questions: What exactly are "key digits" — are they specifically the odd digits of n?
Is the "return 0 if all digits are even" rule the same condition as "no key digits found"?
Is n guaranteed to be a positive integer with at least one digit?
Are digits considered only in the base-10 decimal representation?
If n is a single digit, is that digit itself evaluated as a potential key digit?
Does "product" mean multiplying only the odd digits together, ignoring even ones entirely?
If 0 happens to be one of the digits but isn't a "key" (odd) digit, does it affect the product at all?
Should n=0 be handled as a special edge case?
answers: Yes, key digits are the odd digits of n.
Yes, that's the same condition — no key (odd) digits means the product defaults to 0.
Yes, n is a positive integer with at least one digit.
Yes, a single digit is evaluated on its own parity.
Yes, multiply only the odd digits; even digits are ignored (not treated as 0-multipliers).
No, 0 isn't odd so it's excluded and doesn't affect the product.
n=0 isn't applicable since n is a positive integer.
